newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-HILL MAKES WAY FOR YOUNG TALENT.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL MAKES WAY FOR YOUNG TALENT.

text.p: Young drivers headed by Jacques Villeneuve and Heinz-Harald Frentzen are set to play key roles as Formula One looks forward to a cash boom over the next decade with the spread of pay-per-view digital television.
The departure of newly-crowned world drivers' champion Damon Hill from Williams to the TWR Arrows team for the 1997 season is the signal for a new breed of racers to make their mark.

Canadian Villeneuve, Germany's Frentzen, David Coulthard and fellow Briton Eddie Irvine, and Finland's Mika Hakkinen are the men most likely to take on Hill and former world champion Michael Schumacher, whose younger brother Ralf is also entering the fray.
Villeneuve apart, this generation of talent used 1996 as a transitional year, which helped give Hill his opportunity to land the title.
Villeneuve, eschewing the need for transition, came into Formula One as the IndyCar champion and went straight for the title, finishing runner-up.
German influence is also expected to grow next season with the introduction of Schumacher junior, Mercedes-Benz's commitment to success with McLaren and Frentzen's switch to Williams from Sauber.

The likely arrival of more German drivers and, possibly, BMW engines at Williams in succession to Renault, also hint at an era of German dominance after Japan's Honda and France's Renault dominated the late 1980s and early 1990s.

In 1996, during which Renault announced they will withdraw from Formula One at the end of 1997, Hill not only stamped his authority on the racing track, by winning eight of the 16 grands prix, but he also dispelled the myth that nice guys cannot win in the ruthless world of Formula One.

His championship success was achieved without any resort to foul play, psychological warfare or team assistance, even if his fallibility did unexpectedly allow Villeneuve to remain in contention much longer than expected in his debut season.

"He fully deserved his title," said FIA vice-president Bernie Ecclestone. "But I am not so sure he would have deserved it if he had won it last year. He has worked well, but I would have liked to have seen him next year in a car in which he could defend his crown.

"Having said that, I think Tom (Walkinshaw, owner of TWR Arrows) is a very capable person and he always manages to do what is necessary to do what he wants to achieve. So, I am sure that is what he will do again."

Ecclestone said he felt the sport had recovered fully this year from the damage it suffered to its image in 1994 following the deaths of Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger and a widespread outcry for improved safety.

"Anyone who thinks to the contrary must be crazy," he said. "Just look at our record which is incredible when you think of the number of accidents there are. I don't know how many people have got killed in rallies this year, but it is a lot and nobody says anything.
"I used to say, years ago, how many Formula Ford guys do you have to kill to equal one F1 guy's death before people start screaming. We are probably the safest sport there is."

Ecclestone confirmed that he believed the introduction of digital television in parts of Europe this year would be followed by its spread at such a rate that it would give Formula One financial security, particularly for the smaller teams.
"That is what I think will happen eventually. I don't think we will ever lose tobacco revenue, but I am sure that the whole thing will be scaled down.

"Not just tobacco backing, but sponsorship in general. The new revenue from TV will help us to compensate. More important to us than replacing the existing sponsors is that it will certainly allow the smaller teams, those that are in trouble finding sponsors, to raise their game.
"If they have a lot of money and have the right people, then we will have eight competitive teams rather than four or five in the future."
